Drama is the genre that builds civilizations. Action thrills. Comedy relieves. Horror warns. But drama is the genre that teaches us what to value -- what a good life looks like, what courage costs, what love demands, and what failure means. A culture's dramas are its moral operating system made visible. They are how a society tells itself which sacrifices are noble, which ambitions are hollow, and which relationships are worth dying for. If you want to understand what a civilization believes, do not read its political speeches. Watch its most popular dramas. The speeches lie. The dramas cannot.

For most of cinema history, Hollywood dramas reflected broadly traditional values. Honor mattered. Sacrifice was rewarded. Evil was recognizable and opposition to it was mandatory. Fathers were not punchlines. Faith was not pathology. The individual was responsible for his choices. These were not political positions. They were the water the culture swam in, so thoroughly assumed that no one thought to name them. A drama simply worked or it did not, and a drama that worked almost always worked because it connected viewers to something they recognized as true about the human condition.

The last two decades have reversed this. Contemporary prestige drama now treats traditional values as problems to be solved rather than foundations to be built upon. The father is the villain. Faith is the trauma. Honor is a mask for predation. Sacrifice is internalized oppression. The individual is a vector of systemic forces and his choices were never really his. This inversion has become so thorough that a young viewer who only watched Oscar-nominated dramas from the last ten years would conclude that the family is a prison, marriage is a negotiation between unequals, and any institution older than a tech startup is irredeemably corrupt.

This list is the counterargument. It ranks the 20 most traditional drama films in the VirtueVigil database, sorted from most traditional to least. These are films where the moral architecture is intact: where sacrifice means something, where evil is not ambiguous, where fathers and faith and institutions are capable of good, and where the audience is invited to admire rather than deconstruct. Every entry links to the full VirtueVigil review with complete category breakdowns, parental guidance, content warnings, and scoring methodology. Rankings are determined by VirtueVigil's dual-metric system: Traditional Score measures traditional values present, Woke Score measures ideological content, and Margin is the gap. These 20 films represent the best that drama has to offer viewers who want to be moved without being manipulated.

VirtueVigil has reviewed 269 drama films and shows. These are the 20 most traditional dramas in the database.

#1. The Passion of the Christ (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 45.29 WOKE: 0 MARGIN: +45.0 TRAD

Genre: Biblical Drama • Platform: Theatrical (Newmarket Films / Icon Productions) • Year: 2004

Mel Gibson did not make a movie. He made an act of witness. The Passion of the Christ begins in Gethsemane, in the dark, with Jesus already in agony. There is no backstory, no context for the uninitiated. Gibson assumes you know the story. If you do not, the film will not hold your hand. This is a devotional work, not an introduction. It is aimed at believers who want to feel, at a level that comfortable Sunday-morning Christianity has long forgotten, what the crucifixion cost. The violence is not gratuitous. It is the point. Gibson understood that you cannot soften the Passion and still have the Passion. At +45.0 traditional margin with a woke score of zero, The Passion of the Christ is the most traditional drama in the VirtueVigil database by a wide margin. No other film comes close. It is a direct, unapologetic, physically overwhelming presentation of the central event of Christianity, and it makes no concessions to secular sensibilities. Parents should know the R rating is earned entirely through the graphic depiction of Christ's suffering. This is not a film for children. It is a film for believers who are ready to be confronted with what their faith cost.

#2. Reagan (2024)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 44.28 WOKE: 2.4 MARGIN: +42.0 TRAD

Genre: Biography/Drama/History • Platform: Theatrical • Year: 2024

Reagan is not a biopic. It is a monument. Sean McNamara's film, 14 years in the making and shot on a $25 million budget, does not attempt to understand Ronald Reagan. It does not wrestle with his contradictions, interrogate his failures, or explore the human complexity behind the myth. It worships him. Every frame, every musical cue, every narrative choice is designed to reinforce a single thesis: Ronald Reagan was a great man who saved America. Dennis Quaid plays Reagan with evident affection, and the film structures its storytelling through the eyes of a former KGB agent who spent his career tracking Reagan and ultimately concluded that Reagan's moral clarity was the weapon the Soviet Union could not defend against. At +42.0 traditional margin, this is the most ideologically forceful traditional drama in the database after The Passion of the Christ. Parents should know this is an unapologetically celebratory film that will frustrate viewers looking for critical distance and delight viewers who believe Reagan deserves exactly this kind of treatment.

#3. The Shawshank Redemption (1994)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 47.32 WOKE: 5.18 MARGIN: +42.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / Prison • Platform: Theaters / Home Video / Streaming • Year: 1994

The Shawshank Redemption is the most conservative film ever to be voted the greatest movie of all time, and the fact that it holds that title on IMDb despite containing not a single progressive message should tell you something about what audiences actually value when politics is removed from the equation. Andy Dufresne is wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. He is sent to Shawshank State Penitentiary for two consecutive life sentences. The system has failed him completely. The warden is corrupt. The guards are brutal. The legal mechanisms that should have freed him are indifferent. Every progressive argument about systemic injustice is right there on the surface, available for the film to make. Frank Darabont's adaptation of Stephen King's novella makes none of them. Instead, it tells a story about individual resilience, the redemptive power of hope, male friendship as a moral force, and the idea that a man's character is his destiny. Andy does not wait for the system to save him. He saves himself through patience, intelligence, and an unbroken belief that he deserves to be free. At +42.0 traditional margin with a 47.32 traditional score -- the highest raw traditional score of any film on this list -- Shawshank proves that audiences are hungry for stories about hope, resilience, and friendship when Hollywood gets out of the way and lets them work.

#4. Miracle (2004)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 37.38 WOKE: 1.4 MARGIN: +36.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / Sports / History • Director: Gavin O'Connor • Cast: Kurt Russell, Patricia Clarkson, Noah Emmerich • Year: 2004

Miracle has the easiest setup in sports film history. You already know the ending. The 1980 US Olympic hockey team beating the Soviet Union is one of the most famous moments in American sports. The miracle is not a spoiler. Everyone knows. So the film has to be about something else. And it is: Herb Brooks, played by Kurt Russell in one of the most underrated performances of the 2000s. Brooks is not warm. He is not likeable in the conventional sense. He pushes his players past what they think they can endure because he knows what they are about to face and they do not. The film's portrait of leadership is deeply traditional: the leader's job is not to be loved but to prepare his people for what is coming, even when preparation looks like cruelty to everyone watching. At +36.0 traditional margin, Miracle earns its place as one of the most ideologically sound sports dramas ever made. It is about America, specifically, without apology. The Soviets are the villains. The American system is worth defending. And the men who wore the jersey earned what they achieved through sacrifice that the film does not soften or sentimentalize.

#5. American Sniper (2014)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 36.6 WOKE: 2.45 MARGIN: +34.0 TRAD

Genre: Action / Biography / Drama • Platform: Theatrical (Warner Bros.) • Year: 2014

Chris Kyle is from Texas. He grows up hunting with his father, absorbing lessons about wolves, sheep, and sheepdogs. His father teaches him that there are three kinds of people in this world, and that the Kyles are sheepdogs. This is not complicated. American Sniper knows exactly what it is from its opening frames and delivers on that promise for 132 minutes without flinching or apologizing. Clint Eastwood made this film at 84 years old and it is among the most confident directorial efforts of his career. Bradley Cooper transformed physically and psychologically into Kyle, and the film refuses to pathologize its subject. Kyle is not traumatized by killing. He is traumatized by the people he could not save. The distinction is subtle and the film trusts the audience to understand it without being told. At +34.0 traditional margin, American Sniper is one of the highest-grossing traditional dramas ever made ($547 million worldwide), a fact that the industry spent the following decade pretending was an anomaly rather than a market signal.

#6. Hoosiers (1986)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 34.51 WOKE: 2.75 MARGIN: +32.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / Sports • Director: David Anspaugh • Cast: Gene Hackman, Barbara Hershey, Dennis Hopper • Year: 1986

If you want to explain to someone what a traditional sports film looks like, you show them Hoosiers. That is it. Discussion over. Coach Norman Dale (Gene Hackman) arrives in the tiny Indiana town of Hickory under a cloud. He has a past. He lost a job. He did something he cannot fully undo. The town does not want him. The parents resent him. The best player on the team will not play for him. He has to earn everything. That is the film's moral architecture: authority is not automatically respected, it must be earned through competence and character. Hoosiers does not sneer at the small town it depicts. It does not mock the basketball-as-religion culture of rural Indiana. It takes the community seriously as a community -- flawed, stubborn, capable of cruelty and capable of grace. Gene Hackman gives one of the finest performances of his career. Dennis Hopper earned an Oscar nomination as Shooter, the town drunk who finds redemption through his role as assistant coach. At +32.0 traditional margin, this is the template. Every sports drama since has borrowed from it.

#7. 12 Angry Men (1957)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 30.59 WOKE: 0 MARGIN: +31.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / Crime • Director: Sidney Lumet • Cast: Henry Fonda, Lee J. Cobb, Ed Begley, E.G. Marshall • Year: 1957

12 Angry Men is 96 minutes of men arguing in one room, with no action, no romance, no special effects, and a cast of twelve actors most modern audiences could not name. It is also one of the greatest films ever made. Sidney Lumet's feature debut, adapted from Reginald Rose's teleplay, is so tightly constructed and so morally urgent that you will not notice the lack of anything else. A young man is on trial for murder. The evidence appears overwhelming. Eleven jurors vote guilty. Juror 8, played by Henry Fonda, votes not guilty -- not because he believes the defendant is innocent, but because he believes the evidence deserves more than five minutes of consideration before sending a man to die. The film's traditionalism is not partisan. It is deeper than politics. It is about the dignity of the individual, the moral obligation to take responsibility seriously, and the danger of letting prejudice substitute for judgment. At +31.0 traditional margin with a woke score of zero, 12 Angry Men earns its place as the oldest film on this list and one of the most durable. It has not aged because it is not about its era. It is about something permanent.

#8. 13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghazi (2016)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 32.34 WOKE: 1.7 MARGIN: +31.0 TRAD

Genre: Action / War / Historical Drama • Director: Michael Bay • Cast: John Krasinski, James Badge Dale, Pablo Schreiber • Year: 2016

On September 11, 2012, Islamic militants attacked the US diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya. Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and Foreign Service Officer Sean Smith were killed. Two CIA contractors, Tyrone Woods and Glen Doherty, died in a mortar attack on the CIA annex after fighting through the night. The six-man Global Response Staff team that responded did so after being told to stand down by their chain of command. They went anyway. Michael Bay made this film with unusual restraint. The action sequences are characteristically massive, but the film earns them. It spends significant time establishing these men as men: their families, their humor, their reasons for being in Libya. At +31.0 traditional margin, 13 Hours is both a war film and an indictment of institutional cowardice. It argues that the men on the ground understood the moral situation better than the people in Washington who were paid to understand it, and that when the order came to do nothing, the right response was disobedience. Parents should know this is an intense, combat-heavy film with sustained violence. It is also a tribute to men who did the right thing when doing the right thing was the hardest option.

#9. Gladiator (2000)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 32.2 WOKE: 1.7 MARGIN: +31.0 TRAD

Genre: Action / Adventure / Drama • Platform: Theatrical (DreamWorks / Universal) • Year: 2000

Maximus is a general. He commands the armies of Rome, wins battles for a dying emperor, and wants nothing more than to go home to his farm in Spain, to his wife, to his son, to the smell of wheat and horses in the morning. Marcus Aurelius tells him he wants Maximus to succeed him, to restore Rome to a republic, to give power back to the Senate. Then Commodus finds out. Gladiator is twenty-five years old and it still hits like a fist to the chest. This is one of those rare blockbusters where every element is working at the same level: Russell Crowe's wounded physicality, Joaquin Phoenix's trembling pathetic menace, Hans Zimmer's career-defining score, Ridley Scott's command of scale and momentum. At +31.0 traditional margin, Gladiator earns its place through its unwavering commitment to honor as a real force. Maximus does not fight for revenge, though revenge is available. He fights for the idea of Rome that Marcus Aurelius believed in. He dies for it. The film believes in that sacrifice. It is not ironic about it. It is not embarrassed by it. It is a four-quadrant blockbuster that treats honor, loyalty, and the afterlife with complete sincerity, and it earned $465 million worldwide because audiences were hungry for exactly that.

#10. The Death of Robin Hood (2026)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 34.46 WOKE: 5.9 MARGIN: +29.0 TRAD

Genre: Thriller / Drama / Historical • Director: Michael Sarnoski • Cast: Hugh Jackman, Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgard • Year: 2026

The Death of Robin Hood is a medieval Christian film about a mass murderer who finds redemption through confession, forgiveness, and sacrificial death. A24 did not make a woke Robin Hood. They made a film that takes sin seriously, treats forgiveness as the hardest thing a person can do, and ends with a man choosing to die so a child can have a future. Hugh Jackman plays an aging Robin Hood who has outlived his legend and accumulated a ledger of violence that weighs on him with physical gravity. Jodie Comer plays Sister Brigid, a nun who becomes his confessor and moral anchor. The film's depiction of Christian faith is notably serious: confession is treated as a sacrament with real power, forgiveness is presented as genuinely transformative rather than therapeutic, and death is not the end. At +29.0 traditional margin, this is the most surprising entry in the top ten -- an A24 production that turned out to be one of the most traditionally grounded dramas of the year. Parents should know this is a violent film about a violent man seeking peace. It earns its medieval setting in every sense.

#11. A Great Awakening (2026)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 28.7 WOKE: 0.35 MARGIN: +28.0 TRAD

Genre: History / Drama / Faith • Director: Joshua Enck • Cast: John Paul Sneed, Jonathan Blair • Year: 2026

A Great Awakening tells the story of the unlikely friendship between Benjamin Franklin and George Whitefield, the itinerant preacher whose revivals sparked the First Great Awakening in colonial America. Franklin was a deist and a skeptic. Whitefield was the most famous evangelist of his era, drawing crowds of tens of thousands in an age without amplification. The two men disagreed on nearly everything theological and agreed on nearly everything about human dignity, civic virtue, and the necessity of moral character for a free society to function. Director Joshua Enck treats both men with respect -- Franklin is not a cartoon skeptic, Whitefield is not a cartoon zealot -- and the film's argument is that the American founding drew strength from both the Enlightenment and the Awakening, not one at the expense of the other. At +28.0 traditional margin with a near-zero woke score of 0.35, this is faith-based filmmaking that respects its audience's intelligence. Parents should take their families, their small groups, and the skeptic who thinks faith stories are all saccharine.

#12. Rocky (1976)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 29.54 WOKE: 1.4 MARGIN: +28.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / Sports • Director: John G. Avildsen • Cast: Sylvester Stallone, Talia Shire, Burt Young, Carl Weathers • Year: 1976

Rocky is 50 years old and it still works. That is not a small thing. Most films that win Best Picture feel like artifacts within a decade. Rocky feels like it was made last year. Sylvester Stallone wrote himself a part. He was broke, unknown, and turned down $350,000 to sell the script without the acting role attached. Then he made one of the most enduring American films about the dignity of going the distance. Rocky Balboa is not smart. He is not talented in the way Apollo Creed is talented. What he has is the refusal to quit. The film treats that refusal as genuinely noble -- not as toxic masculinity, not as internalized oppression, not as a coping mechanism for poverty. It says that getting up one more time than you get knocked down is a definition of courage. At +28.0 traditional margin, Rocky is the film that launched a franchise and a philosophy. The training montage, the meat locker, the stairs, the final freeze frame -- these are cultural touchstones because the film earned them, not because they were marketed. Parents should know this is a PG film with some violence and adult themes, but it is fundamentally about a man trying to prove he is not a bum. Few films have made that case with more sincerity.

#13. Saving Private Ryan (1998)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 30.8 WOKE: 2.5 MARGIN: +28.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama / War • Platform: Theatrical (DreamWorks / Paramount) • Year: 1998

The first twenty-five minutes of Saving Private Ryan are among the most important minutes in the history of American cinema. Not because they are the most technically impressive war footage ever shot, though they are that. Because they do something that almost no war film before or since has done: they make you understand, at a cellular level, what those men went through on June 6, 1944. The Omaha Beach sequence is not entertainment. It is a moral argument delivered through sensory overload. Steven Spielberg then pivots to a rescue mission that could be described as a contrived plot device and instead becomes an examination of duty, sacrifice, and the question of what one man's life is worth. Captain Miller (Tom Hanks) does not want this mission. He does not believe in it. His squad does not believe in it. They do it anyway because orders are orders and their country asked. At +28.0 traditional margin, Saving Private Ryan is a war film that treats military service as honorable, sacrifice as meaningful, and the American project as worth the cost. Parents should know the violence is graphic and sustained. This is not a film for children. It is a film for anyone who needs to understand what was given so they could live free.

#14. Sound of Hope: The Story of Possum Trot (2024)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 29.82 WOKE: 2.0 MARGIN: +28.0 TRAD

Genre: Biography / Drama • Director: Joshua Weigel • Cast: Demetrius Grosse, Nika King, Elizabeth Mitchell • Year: 2024

The story of Possum Trot, Texas, is one of the most extraordinary stories in American religious life in the last thirty years. A small church. A community that most people in most coastal cities could not find on a map. And over twenty years, 22 families in that church adopted 77 children from the state foster system, most of them children with trauma histories so severe that the professional system had given up on them. Sound of Hope tells this story without irony, without condescension, and without the reflexive skepticism that secular Hollywood would bring to a story about faith-motivated action. The families of Possum Trot did what they did because their pastor asked them to, and their pastor asked because he believed Jesus meant what He said about caring for the least of these. The film takes that motivation seriously. At +28.0 traditional margin, this is faith-based filmmaking that respects both its subjects and its audience. Parents should know this is a film about children who have suffered genuine trauma. The content is emotionally intense rather than violent, but it earns its PG-13 rating through the weight of its subject matter.

#15. Risen (2016)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 28.6 WOKE: 1.8 MARGIN: +27.0 TRAD

Genre: Biblical Drama / Historical Epic • Director: Kevin Reynolds • Cast: Joseph Fiennes, Tom Felton, Cliff Curtis • Year: 2016

Risen takes the smartest approach to biblical drama available: it tells the Easter story through the eyes of a skeptic. Joseph Fiennes plays Clavius, a Roman tribune stationed in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate. He is a military man, a pragmatist, a functionary of empire. When the body of the crucified Yeshua disappears from its tomb, Clavius is ordered to find it and suppress the growing rumor of resurrection. What follows is a detective story set in first-century Judea, and it works because Fiennes sells Clavius's incremental transformation from investigator to witness. He does not convert because he wants to. He converts because the evidence leaves him no alternative. At +27.0 traditional margin, Risen is biblical filmmaking that respects the intelligence of believers and skeptics alike. Cliff Curtis plays Yeshua with warmth and authority, and the film's restraint -- it shows the crucifixion without dwelling on it, the resurrection without over-explaining it -- makes its argument more powerful than a more didactic approach would have achieved. Parents should know this is PG-13 for biblical violence and thematic material. It is one of the best Easter films available for families with teenagers.

#16. Fury (2014)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 31.08 WOKE: 4.9 MARGIN: +26.0 TRAD

Genre: War / Drama • Director: David Ayer • Cast: Brad Pitt, Shia LaBeouf, Logan Lerman, Michael Pena, Jon Bernthal • Year: 2014

Fury is a war film made by someone who actually cares about war -- not the spectacle of it, but the weight of it. David Ayer spent years researching this project, talking to veterans, studying the European theater in the final months of fighting. April 1945 in Germany is a specific kind of hell: the war is effectively over, everyone knows it, and men are still dying for ground that will be surrendered by armistice. The five-man crew of the Sherman tank Fury -- Wardaddy (Brad Pitt), Bible (Shia LaBeouf), Gordo (Michael Pena), Coon-Ass (Jon Bernthal), and the new replacement Norman (Logan Lerman) -- have been together since North Africa. They are not heroes in the conventional sense. They are survivors, and survival has cost them most of their humanity. The film's moral center is Bible, who quotes scripture while manning the main gun, and whose faith is treated as the thing that has kept him from becoming what the war wants to turn him into. At +26.0 traditional margin, Fury earns its place through its refusal to glamorize war while simultaneously refusing to apologize for fighting it. The enemy is evil. The cause is just. The cost is terrible. All three things can be true, and the film holds them in tension without flinching.

#17. Brave the Dark (2025)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 26.18 WOKE: 1.35 MARGIN: +25.0 TRAD

Genre: Drama • Platform: Theatrical (Angel Studios) • Year: 2025

Brave the Dark is the kind of film that almost does not get made anymore. An Angel Studios release directed by Damian Harris and starring his brother Jared Harris as Stan Deen, a high school drama teacher in 1980s New Holland, Pennsylvania who discovers one of his students is living out of a car. Stan bails Nate out of jail, offers him a bed, and over the course of months becomes the father figure Nate never had. That is the whole plot. The film does not complicate it with irony or subversion. It tells a story about a man who saw a kid in trouble and decided to help, and it trusts that the story is enough. At +25.0 traditional margin with a near-zero woke score of 1.35, Brave the Dark represents something valuable in the current media landscape: a drama that believes in the possibility of genuine goodness without needing to interrogate it, deconstruct it, or reveal it as a cover for something darker. Jared Harris brings real craft to a role that could have been sentimental, and the film's refusal to apologize for its sincerity is its greatest strength. Parents looking for a drama they can watch with teenagers without navigating ideological minefields will find exactly that here.

#18. The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 25.9 WOKE: 1.0 MARGIN: +25.0 TRAD

Genre: Adventure / Fantasy / Drama • Platform: Theatrical (New Line Cinema) • Year: 2001

The Fellowship of the Ring is one of the most important films of the twenty-first century, and its importance has nothing to do with its box office or its technical achievements, which were considerable. J.R.R. Tolkien was a devout Catholic who wrote The Lord of the Rings as a fundamentally Christian work, and Peter Jackson's adaptation -- while stripping some of the overt religious references -- preserved the moral architecture intact. Good and evil are real, distinguishable, and in absolute opposition. Power corrupts absolutely. The smallest and weakest among us may be the vessel of salvation. Friendship is a force that evil cannot account for. Sacrifice is not a metaphor. At +25.0 traditional margin, Fellowship earns its place through the sheer weight of its moral seriousness. The Council of Elrond scene alone -- where representatives of races who have spent centuries distrusting each other volunteer to walk into certain death together -- is more ideologically traditional than the entire output of most modern studios in a calendar year. Parents should know this trilogy is the gold standard for family viewing that takes children seriously as moral beings.

#19. The Lion King (1994)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 24.85 WOKE: 1.05 MARGIN: +24.0 TRAD

Genre: Animated / Drama / Musical • Platform: Theatrical (Disney) • Year: 1994

Before Disney decided its animated legacy was a problem to be apologized for, the studio made The Lion King -- a film about a young prince who must accept the responsibility he was born to carry. Simba's journey is not about discovering his authentic self against the constraints of tradition. It is about accepting that tradition -- the circle of life, the legacy of his father, the duty of kingship -- is the source of meaning, not its obstacle. Mufasa's ghost does not tell Simba to follow his heart. He tells Simba to remember who he is. That distinction is the difference between a traditional moral framework and a therapeutic one, and The Lion King commits to it completely. At +24.0 traditional margin, the film remains one of Disney's most enduring achievements precisely because its moral architecture is so sound. The villain is a murderer who rules through fear and manipulation. The hero must reclaim his birthright not for personal glory but for the good of all. The film takes death seriously: Mufasa's death in the stampede is as devastating now as it was in 1994. Parents should know this is family entertainment at its finest -- a film that teaches children about duty, courage, and the weight of responsibility while entertaining them completely.

#20. American Underdog (2021)

STRONGLY TRADITIONAL TRAD: 26.04 WOKE: 2.0 MARGIN: +24.0 TRAD

Genre: Biography / Drama / Sports • Platform: Theatrical (Lionsgate) • Year: 2021

Kurt Warner's story is ridiculous. Undrafted out of Northern Iowa. Cut by the Green Bay Packers. Stocking shelves at a Hy-Vee grocery store in Cedar Falls, Iowa, for $5.50 an hour. Playing arena football for the Iowa Barnstormers. And then, in 1999, becoming the NFL MVP and leading the St. Louis Rams to a Super Bowl victory in one of the greatest Cinderella stories in sports history. American Underdog tells this story straight, and it works because the story does not need embellishment. Zachary Levi plays Warner with the earnestness the role demands. Anna Paquin plays Brenda, Warner's wife, whose son from a previous relationship is blind and brain-damaged -- a detail that in a more cynical film would be mined for inspiration-porn but here is treated with dignity as part of the Warners' actual life together. At +24.0 traditional margin, American Underdog is a faith-based sports drama that respects its audience enough to let the story speak for itself. The Warners' Christian faith is central without being preachy. Kurt's perseverance is presented as a function of character rather than luck. The film's message is clear and traditional: talent matters less than persistence, love matters more than success, and God's timing is not ours. Parents should know this is a PG film suitable for the whole family.
